questions.q: What is the programme mainly about?
options: How to win every argument with friends and family
Whether disagreeing is good and how to do it better
Why politicians in parliament never agree on anything
How couples' therapy works for married people
questions.why: Sam says they're discussing 'Is it good to disagree?' and they hear tips for disagreeing better.

questions.q: Why does Rob say “No, we won't!” at the start?
options: He doesn't want to talk about the topic
He thinks the programme is too short
He is angry with Sam
He is disagreeing on purpose as a joke
questions.why: He says he feels better for having that little disagreement, which proves it's good to disagree.

options: He says it should be 'five minutes', not six
He refuses to answer the quiz question at all
He talks too much and doesn't let Sam speak
He disagrees with everything that Sam says
questions.why: Rob corrects Sam's 'next six minutes' to five, and Sam says he is focusing too much on small details.

questions.q: According to Esther Perel, what happens in a bad disagreement?
options: Both people finally agree to reach a compromise
Nobody says what they really think about the issue
One person acts superior and shows contempt
People stop listening to each other and just leave
questions.why: She says in a battle one person is on top of the other, with contempt, thinking the other is lesser.

questions.q: Which tip for disagreeing better does the podcast Seriously give?
options: Always aim for the middle ground
Listen carefully and aim for empathy
Avoid speaking truthfully
Make sure you agree at the end
questions.why: Rob says it suggests speaking truthfully, listening intently and aiming for empathy.

questions.q: What convinced Douglas Alexander that disagreement is necessary?
options: His years as an elected politician
A book on arguing that he read at university
His early work as a family therapist
A big family argument at Christmas
questions.why: He says a couple of decades as an elected politician convinced him disagreement is necessary.

questions.q: According to Douglas Alexander, what would happen if society valued politeness over truth and justice?
options: People would be happier
There would be fewer wars
Politicians would be more honest
Society would stop developing
questions.why: He says it would simply be 'a recipe for stagnation'.

questions.q: What does Sam add to Douglas Alexander's advice?
options: Disagreements should be kept short and simple
People should avoid difficult topics like politics
Disagreeing should be done politely and with respect
People should always compromise in the end
questions.why: Sam says, “I would add that this should be done politely and with respect.”
